brief.notification_title: Relief bounce meets hot jobs; Dec hike odds 77%
brief.market_summary: Stocks are bouncing after Thursday's AI-led rout, when the S&P fell 4.36% and the Nasdaq 5.52%. At 12:42 ET the S&P 500 is up 0.57% at 7,395.87 and the Nasdaq up 1.18%, led by semis (SMH +2.58%), and the VIX is down 14% at 24.19. October payrolls came in at 165K against about 65K expected, which lifted December hike odds to roughly 77% and the 2-year about 6bp. Strong productivity and falling unit labor costs kept the 10-year at 4.85% (+1.6bp) and the 30-year flat. Brent is $97.51 and heading for a 12–17% weekly loss on Iran-peace hopes after the Democratic midterm sweep. Bitcoin, at $75,593, has sat out the equity bounce and is near an 11-week low after spot ETF outflows and more than $1B of liquidations.
brief.since_last: Thursday's selloff deepened into the close: S&P −4.36%, Dow −3.44%, Nasdaq −5.52%. The Nasdaq closed in correction, and StockTitan called it the worst day since April 2025 (n41, n55). Earnings after the close split sharply. Airbnb, Cloudflare and JFrog beat and raised and jumped 12–35%; DraftKings, Axon and Atlassian missed and fell 15–26%. This morning Moderna beat and raised, and Lam Research announced a $25B buyback. October payrolls beat every forecast: +165K, unemployment 4.1%, wages +0.4% m/m, with +84K of revisions. December hike odds went from 68.4% to 76.8% (n44, n46). The same morning, Q3 productivity rose 3.6% and unit labor costs fell 0.7%, which is the inflation-friendly part of the data. The dollar is up 0.6% and gold down 1%. Brent briefly topped $100 overnight on tanker attacks (n170, n174) but is back at $97.5. Bitcoin hit an 11-week low near $75K. Spot BTC ETFs lost $430M on Thursday and about $870M over November's first four sessions, and there is a $3.1B overhang of stolen Binance crypto that hasn't been laundered yet (n111). None of the previous brief's limit orders appear to have filled.

economic_data.previous: Aug revised to 186K; Aug–Sep revisions net +84K
economic_data.takeaway: It beat all 79 Bloomberg forecasts and lifted December hike odds to about 77%. Reuters had the 2Y up 6bp at 4.52% and the dollar is up 0.6%. That is a headwind for long-duration tech and for crypto.
There is no labor slack building, which removes the Fed's main reason to pause the gradual hiking path (n180).
Wages beat, but y/y growth of 3.1% still trails inflation (n115). That makes this a firm labor market rather than a wage-price spiral.
This is what the market is underrating. Output is paying for the wage gains, so they aren't inflationary, which helps explain why the 10Y rose only about 2bp and the 30Y was flat.
Layoffs remain low (4-week average 194.75K), consistent with the payrolls strength.
This is a three-month high, but interviews closed 2 Nov, before the rout and the midterms, so it is stale. 1Y inflation expectations of 4.3% keep the Fed vigilant.
Services are cooling at the margin (S&P Global services 56.1 vs 57.9 expected) and price pressure eased slightly. GDPNow slipped to 3.4% from 3.7%. That mildly supports buying bonds near 5%.
The crude draw was smaller than expected, but the large distillate draw fits the global diesel squeeze (n59). Physical product markets stay tight even as futures price in peace.

brief.instructor_take: Today's bounce is relief, not repair. Read Thursday and Friday together. AI leadership broke on a policy shock and an AI credit shock, and the data then gave the Fed every reason to keep hiking: payrolls tripled consensus and December odds are about 77%. The crowd is pointing to the VIX spike as a buy signal (n31). My view is that those signals work best when the Fed can come to the rescue, and this Fed is leaning the other way. What I think the market is missing is the productivity report: +3.6% with unit labor costs −0.7%. That is why the 30-year didn't move on a blowout jobs number. It tells me the long end is a better place to add risk than the high-multiple end of the equity market. Also look at the monthly sector table: health care +10%, staples +9%, financials +6%, tech −17%. This is a rotation, and the right move is to adjust concentration rather than abandon stocks. My positioning: sell some tech into strength, fund quality defensives at disciplined prices, and keep dry powder in bills yielding about 4% for a CPI-plus-auctions week that could hand us 10-year yields near 5%. I'm standing aside on oil, where the outcome depends on one Iran headline, and on crypto, where BTC can't rally even on a green Nasdaq day. I'd change my mind on tech if CPI comes in soft and CoreWeave and Applied Materials show financing and orders holding up.

top_ideas.title: Trim tech overweight into the bounce, lower limits
top_ideas.one_liner: Sell 1/3 of tech overweight at XLK $168–170; hike odds 77%
top_ideas.thesis: Thursday's roughly 8% XLK drop was a breakdown, and the macro turned more hawkish today, with December hike odds near 77%. AI credit is also under stress, with CoreWeave bonds above 16%. I'm using the short-covering bounce to cut concentration at a 38–50% retracement rather than waiting for the old $172–174 limits.
top_ideas.reasoning: I see Thursday as a breakdown, not a dip. XLK fell about 8% in one session, from roughly $177 to about $162 by my estimate from today's +1.3%, and the Nasdaq closed in correction. Today's bounce looks like short covering, with SMH +2.6% and the VIX −14%, but the AI story got weaker overnight: CoreWeave bonds yield over 16% (n14), Anthropic's IPO valuation is being marked down (n33), and voters backed data-center limits (n7). Add a 165K payrolls print that lifted the 2-year about 6bp, and higher short rates hit long-duration growth multiples hardest. The concept I'm applying is retracement. After a breakdown, bounces often retrace 38–50% of the drop before sellers return, which on XLK is $168–170, so I'm lowering the limits from $172–174 to give them a realistic chance of filling. A less experienced investor treats this as a call on whether tech is finished. It isn't: chips now trade below the S&P's multiple (n6) and Cloudflare shows demand is real, so I'm reducing concentration and keeping the core. I'm wrong if XLK reclaims $177, which would make Thursday a one-day flush, and a soft CPI plus solid CoreWeave and Applied Materials results would push me that way.

top_ideas.title: Health care: finish the add, never above $184

top_ideas.thesis: Health care held up during the rout (+0.2% on the week vs XLK −8.4%) and the sector's earnings keep beating: Cigna $7.98 vs $7.46, and Moderna beat and raised its outlook. Its cash flows are largely independent of the AI capex cycle and the December hike. I'll complete the position only at a disciplined price because the sector is up 10% in a month.
top_ideas.reasoning: My evidence is relative strength under stress. XLV is +0.2% on the week and +10.1% on the month, while XLK is −8.4% and −16.8%. Earnings back that up: Cigna beat by 7% and Moderna raised 2026 revenue growth guidance to 15–25%. Health care cash flows are much less tied to AI capex or to whether the Fed hikes in December, which is what the portfolio needs while I trim tech. Price is the discipline. After a 10% month defensives are getting crowded, so I won't pay above $184 and would prefer $181–182. A common mistake is buying the defensive sector after it has already worked; the price cap is what protects you, not the sector's defensive label. Humana reported this morning and I don't have the numbers, so read them before Monday, because a guidance cut there is one of my invalidations. I'm wrong if XLV closes below $176, which would mean de-risking has spread to the defensives too.

top_ideas.title: 7–10Y Treasuries only on a back-up toward 5%
top_ideas.one_liner: Buy IEF at $91.20 / $90.60 if CPI and auctions push 10Y to ~5%
top_ideas.thesis: The 10-year barely moved on a payrolls blowout because productivity rose 3.6% and unit labor costs fell 0.7%. December's hike is now mostly priced. A CPI week with $119B of note and bond supply is a classic setup for a temporary yield back-up to 4.95–5.05%, where I want to own intermediate duration.
top_ideas.reasoning: The bond market's reaction today told us something. Payrolls beat every forecast, yet the 10-year rose only about 2bp and the 30-year was flat. The explanation is the productivity release: +3.6% vs 2.8% expected, with unit labor costs −0.7%, so wage gains are being paid for by output, which limits how far the Fed has to go. Hikes push the front end hardest, and with December about 77% priced, a 10-year near 5% would already pay me for much of that risk. I'm not buying at 4.85% because next week brings CPI plus $58B of 3s, $39B of 10s and $22B of 30s. Auctions often need a yield concession, and that is when patient buyers get in. I prefer IEF to TLT because I want about 7–8 years of duration rather than 17: enough to benefit if the equity selloff resumes, but not enough for a sticky-inflation scare to wreck the position. To be candid, one of my original invalidations, payrolls putting a December hike firmly in play, has partly happened. I'm keeping the idea because the long end shrugged it off, but I've tightened the trigger to something measurable. I step aside if the 10Y closes above 5.20%, or if CPI is hot enough that the market starts pricing a faster pace than gradual 25bp steps.

lesson.concept: The Fed reaction function: 'good news is bad news'
lesson.explanation: Markets don't trade the economy directly. They trade what the economy means for the central bank's next move. When the Fed is hiking, strong growth or jobs data raises the odds of more hikes. That lifts short-term yields and the dollar and lowers the present value of assets whose cash flows are far in the future, such as tech, long bonds and crypto. The detail is where the skill lies: you have to check whether the strength is inflationary or not, because that decides whether long-term yields follow short-term ones.
lesson.todays_example: Payrolls of 165K vs 65K moved December hike odds from 68% to 77%. The 2Y rose about 6bp, the dollar 0.6%, gold fell 1%, and BTC couldn't join the equity bounce. Productivity of +3.6% with unit labor costs −0.7% says the strength isn't wage-inflationary, so the 10Y rose only about 2bp and the 30Y didn't move. Even with a hawkish 'good news is bad news' reaction, the curve sorted the data correctly.
